title: Selected Annotations on the Lankavatara Sutra
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: 1. No Gate Is the Dharma Gate 2. The Five Dharmas and the Three Self-Natures

inline.s: 1. No Gate Is the Dharma Gate
2. The Five Dharmas and the Three Self-Natures
3. The Lankavatara King's Request
4. The Meaning of the One Hundred and Eight Phrases
The Lankavatara Sutra is devoted specifically to the essential gateway of the Tathagata's mind-ground; it is an exceedingly important treasure for practice. This sutra has three translations:
1. Liu Song
Gunabhadra (

), whose translation is the Lankavatara Ratna Sutra, in four fascicles. It is also called the four-fascicle Lankavatara Sutra, the Song translation of the Lankavatara Sutra, or simply the "Song translation."

(Liu Song, 420-479 CE) The first dynasty of the Southern Dynasties during the Northern and Southern Dynasties period — Song. Because its rulers were surnamed Liu, it is called Liu Song to distinguish it from the Song dynasty later founded by Zhao Kuangyin.
2. Northern Wei
Bodhiruci (?

), whose translation is the Sutra of Entering Lanka, in ten fascicles. It is also called the ten-fascicle Lankavatara Sutra, the Wei translation of the Lankavatara Sutra, or simply the "Wei translation."
(Northern Wei, 386-534 CE) The first dynasty of the Northern Dynasties during the Northern and Southern Dynasties period — Wei.
3. Tang
Siksananda (

), whose translation is the Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka, in seven fascicles. It is also called the seven-fascicle Lankavatara Sutra, the Tang translation of the Lankavatara Sutra, or simply the "Tang translation."

This Tang translation was made by Siksananda at the command of Empress Wu Zetian. Since the Lankavatara Sutra is "the mysterious pivot of the mind-measure of all Buddhas, the wondrous key to the treasure-caves of all sutras," while Gunabhadra's, terse and archaic in wording, had not circulated widely, and Bodhiruci's was marred by many errors (
chuǎn

, erroneous), she took the Sanskrit original from the palace and asked Siksananda to retranslate it from the original, consulting the two earlier versions and "examining the essential meanings of the three versions." Thus the seven-fascicle Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka came into being. Compared with the first two, the Tang rendering is fluent in phrase and clear in meaning.

(Mind-measure) When the mind gives rise to false imagining and takes all manner of measure of outer objects, this is the mind-measure of ordinary beings; the mind-measure genuinely realized by the Tathagata is far removed from all objects and from all grasping, and dwells in no-mind. This sutra says:
"Who sees all conditioned dharmas / from grasp and grasping free — / that mind-measure of no-mind / is mind-measure to me."

(Mysterious pivot) The hub for grasping the profound meaning of the Way. (Wondrous key) The wondrous key to attaining the Way; "key" means a key. (Examining the essential meanings of the three versions) Thoroughly investigating the essential meaning expounded by the three versions of the sutra (two Chinese translations and one Sanskrit original).

Among these three Chinese translations, the four-fascicle Lankavatara Sutra (the Lankavatara Ratna Sutra) was entrusted by Bodhidharma, the first patriarch of Chan, to the second patriarch Huike, with the words:
"In the land of Han I see no other sutra; let the worthy one practice according to this and naturally attain deliverance from the world."

This is the supreme treasure for transmitting the lamp and sealing the mind; patriarch after patriarch handed it down as the mind-dharma, and possessing great power to gather and transform beings, it circulated most widely. Except for the first chapter, "The Lankavatara King's Request," taken from the Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka, the sutra text in the remaining chapters ("No Gate Is the Dharma Gate," "The Five Dharmas and the Three Self-Natures," "The Meaning of the One Hundred and Eight Phrases," "The Storehouse Consciousness and the Evolving Consciousnesses," "The Realm of the Storehouse Consciousness," "No-Self and the Tathagatagarbha," "Awakening to the Mind's Own Manifestation," "The Great Skillful Means Dharma Gate," and "The Mark of Self-Realized Noble Wisdom") is taken from this translation. When passages from the other two translations are quoted, the Sutra of Entering Lanka is abbreviated as the Wei translation, and the Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka as the Tang translation.
The Lankavatara Sutra — this is the method by which Shakyamuni Buddha himself proclaimed the perfect realization of Buddhahood he had attained (
"the Dharma of the noble wisdom realized by himself"
). Yet the text is abstruse and hard to read. In Su Dongpo's words (Preface to the Lankavatara Ratna Sutra):
"The meaning of the Lankavatara is ever
(zhé, namely)

profound and subtle, while its wording is terse and archaic. Readers may not even be able to punctuate the sentences — how much less can they set aside the text to grasp the meaning, and forget the meaning to awaken the mind?"

(Translation: In the Lankavatara, the meaning is profound and subtle, while the wording is terse and archaic. Readers may not even be able to punctuate it — how much less set aside the text to grasp the meaning, and forget the meaning to awaken the mind?)

(Profound and subtle, miǎo) Deep and refined. (Punctuating sentences) Books in ancient times had no punctuation marks. When reciting, one paused according to the meaning, or also marked the book with circles and dots at the pauses; this was called "punctuating sentences." Such "sentences" were often shorter than what grammar today calls a sentence.
To understand the sutra more easily and deeply, first read
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha
and
The True Nature of All Dharmas
so as to gain a comprehensive understanding of mind, self-nature, tathagatagarbha, and the true nature of all dharmas.

blocks.text: 1. No Gate Is the Dharma Gate

inline.s: Question: Master Mazu said that the Lankavatara Sutra teaches:
"The Buddha's teaching takes mind as its essence; no gate is the dharma gate."
What does this sentence mean?

Answer: "The Buddha's teaching takes mind as its essence" means the Lankavatara Sutra takes mind as its essential doctrine. The entire Lankavatara Ratna Sutra has only one chapter, and its chapter title is: The Mind of All Buddha-Speech. "The mind of all Buddha-speech": all Buddha-speech teaches only this mind. That is to say, all Buddhas proclaim this mind. For

one's own mind is Buddha; all realms are merely what karma evokes and what mind alone manifests. Whether one is in birth-and-death or in nirvana depends entirely on a single turn of mind, and there is no other dharma.
The mind is so important that all Buddhas proclaim it. Master Hanshan said:
"Because
(since)
this sutra points directly to the storehouse consciousness of sentient beings as the tathagatagarbha, revealing the states that appear before us in daily use,
causing one to follow along and observe the mind's own manifestation, and instantly realize the self-realized noble wisdom of all Buddhas
, therefore it is named 'the mind of Buddha-speech.'"
(Notes from the Pavilion for Contemplating the Lankavatara Precious Sutra)
(Only one chapter in the whole) According to Master Hanshan's Notes on Contemplating the Lankavatara Sutra:
"This sutra has forty fascicles. This
(the Lankavatara Sutra that reached our land)
is only one tenth of it."
(The mind of all Buddha-speech) The Tang translation says:
"the mind taught by all Buddhas."

(The consciousness-store is the tathagatagarbha) The consciousness-store and the tathagatagarbha are two states of one body. See the chapter "The Storehouse Consciousness and the Evolving Consciousnesses."

(The mind's own manifestation) "Direct perception" means intuitively knowing that something exists without conceptual thought — direct knowing. (Knowing by inference is "inferential cognition.") Awakening to the mind's own manifestation is like a mirror reflecting objects: knowing the states manifested by one's own mind without conceptual calculation. This sutra says:
"Simply awaken to the mind's own manifestation, and false imagining does not arise; one is peaceful
(same as "steady")
and happy, and worldly affairs cease forever."
The Record of the Mirror of the Source says:

"The Buddha said: 'Simply awaken to the mind's own manifestation, and false imagining does not arise; one is peaceful and happy, and worldly affairs cease forever.' To be peaceful and happy is to be tranquil, wondrous, and constant; for worldly affairs to cease forever is for grasping to be cut off. One may be said to have met with a perfect treasure trove, to have suddenly cut off all seeking, to have reached the nirvana of everlasting bliss, beyond which there is nowhere further to go. At the boundary between ordinary beings and sages, one is as if arrived home; as the reliance of the deluded and the awakened, one has fathomed the root. The Mahaparinirvana Sutra says: 'The vajra treasury lacks nothing.'"
Master Hanshan's Notes on Contemplating the Lankavatara Sutra says:
"Because
(since)
the mind's own manifestation is such that sage and ordinary being are not established and all is negated, thereby revealing
(and thus displaying)
the ultimate meaning of enlightenment within birth and death.'"
Patriarch Bodhidharma's Dharma Gate of Pacifying the Mind says:

"Whoever has a mind that discriminates and calculates the mind's own manifestation — all of it is a dream. If one understands that the mind is quiescent and extinguished, with no place for any thought, this is called right enlightenment."
Master Hanshan also said:
"The chapter "The Mind of Buddha-Speech":
this sutra points directly to the quiescent one mind as its essence, and takes entry by realization of self-realized noble wisdom as its aim
(Supplement to the Lankavatara)
(The Buddha's teaching takes mind as its essence; no gate is the dharma gate) The Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp records:
(Mazu)

One day he addressed the assembly: All of you, each believe that your own mind is Buddha; this mind is the Buddha-mind. Great Master Bodhidharma came from South India to China in person and transmitted the supreme teaching of the one mind, causing you to open to awakening. He also cited passages from the Lankavatara Sutra to seal the mind-ground of sentient beings, fearing that you might be inverted and not believe in this dharma of the mind, which each of you possesses. Therefore the Lankavatara Sutra says:
the Buddha's teaching takes mind as its essence; 'no' gate is the dharma gate.

It also says: One who seeks the dharma should seek nothing; outside the mind there is no other Buddha, and outside the Buddha there is no other mind. Not grasping good, not rejecting evil, relying on neither purity nor defilement
(hù)

, realizing the emptiness of the nature of offenses — thought after thought unattainable, because without self-nature. Therefore the three realms are mind only, and the myriad phenomena are all sealed by the one dharma."
(The myriad phenomena are all sealed by the one dharma)

The myriad phenomena are all stamped with the imprint of the one dharma. (The one dharma seal) Also called the one true-nature seal, or the seal of the true nature of all dharmas. A dharma seal is the seal of the Buddhadharma, the seal of truth passed down from Buddha to Buddha; it is the criterion of the Buddhadharma, and whatever does not accord with it is not Buddhadharma. The Mahayana teachings take the true nature of all dharmas as their foundation; apart from this, it is the teaching of Mara. (The true nature of all dharmas) "True nature" means the actual state of affairs; "the true nature of all dharmas" means the actual state of affairs of all dharmas. The Sutra of the Buddha-Treasury says:
"What is called the true nature of all dharmas? It is that all dharmas are ultimately empty, nothing whatsoever."
The Mahaparinirvana Sutra says:
"All dharmas are like illusions, and the Tathagata, amid them, by the power of skillful means, is unstained and unattached."
The Lotus Sutra says:
"The bodhisattva mahasattva contemplates all dharmas as empty, as they truly are — not inverted, not moved, not retreating, not turning."
(See
The True Nature of All Dharmas
in full.)

(Noble wisdom) The Tathagata's wisdom of the essential nature of the dharma realm — the wisdom that awakens to "all dharmas are originally unborn"; also called the pure dharma-realm wisdom. This sutra says:

"Mahamati, one whose mark of the ultimate self-realized noble wisdom is such that he does not calculate or attach to any mark of dharma, gains the body of the samadhi of illusion, and advances and brings forth conduct at the stage of all Buddhas."
It also says:

"The Buddha told Mahamati: What former sages knew, they transmitted to one another — that false imagining has no nature. The bodhisattva mahasattva, dwelling alone in a quiet place, observes with self-realization, not relying on another, free from the views of false imagining, advances higher and higher, and enters the Tathagata's stage; this is called the mark of self-realized noble wisdom."

No gate is the dharma gate" — "no gate" does not mean that there is no gate. The "no" here is not the "no" of existence and non-existence; it is the true nature of all dharmas that transcends existence and non-existence — originally there is not a single thing. The "gate" here means a path, a key. "No gate is the dharma gate" means:
taking "no" as the path of practice.

In other words, by the principle of the true nature of all dharmas, one shatters the dream of ignorance and perfectly accomplishes the Buddha Way. Then what is used to shatter it? The mind is used to shatter it. Therefore it is said: "The Buddha's teaching takes mind as its essence." In the Lankavatara Sutra, this method of practice, "no," is taught everywhere, and summed up it is:

the five dharmas and the three natures are all empty; the eight consciousnesses and the two selves are both relinquished; the two dharmas of existence and non-existence are entirely transcended; one realizes self-realized noble wisdom and enters the Tathagata's stage.
— This is the main content of the Lankavatara Sutra.

blocks.text: 2. The Five Dharmas and the Three Self-Natures

inline.s: The main content of the Lankavatara Sutra is:

the five dharmas and the three natures are all empty; the eight consciousnesses and the two selves are both relinquished; the two dharmas of existence and non-existence are entirely transcended; one realizes self-realized noble wisdom and enters the Tathagata's stage.
This sutra says:
"The five dharmas and the three self-natures, together with the eight kinds of consciousness, and the two kinds of no-self, comprise the Mahayana
(encompass all of the Great Vehicle)
(Mahayana) Short for Mahayana; rendered in Chinese as the Great Vehicle.
(The five dharmas)

All dharmas can be summed up in five: mark, name, discrimination, right wisdom, and suchness. 1. Mark: the myriad phenomena, whose forms each differ. 2. Name: positing various names based on those marks, in order to express them. 3. Discrimination: thinking about and distinguishing the marks and names of all things, whereby size, height, beauty and ugliness, right and wrong, and so on appear. 4. Right wisdom: the unstained mind and mental factors, far from discrimination, regarding name and mark as mutually external, free from permanence and annihilation, knowing in accordance with principle. 5. Suchness: the realm realized by right wisdom, the essence of true suchness in which mind and object are both quiescent.

The relations among the five dharmas are: based on "mark" one establishes "name"; based on "name" one thinks and calculates ("discrimination"); by "right wisdom" one is free from "discrimination" and realizes "suchness." Among these, "discrimination" goes from delusion into delusion, sinking lower and lower; "right wisdom" goes from awakening into awakening, advancing higher and higher, and enters the Tathagata's stage. In the Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka,

"the Buddha said: Mahamati, the bodhisattva mahasattva, relying on the teachings of the sages, is without discrimination. Dwelling alone in quiet, he observes with self-realization, not awakened by another, free from the views of discrimination, advances higher and higher, and enters the Tathagata's stage. Such practice is called the mark of conduct of self-realized noble wisdom."
(The three natures)

That is, the three self-natures: 1. The self-nature of dependent arising: all dharmas arise depending on various conditions, have no substantial reality, and are merely illusory; hence the self-nature of dependent arising. 2. The self-nature of false imagining: sentient beings are deluded and do not understand that all dharmas are originally empty; they falsely calculate regarding their own bodies and all dharmas, grasping each as truly existent; hence the self-nature of false imagining. 3. The self-nature of perfect accomplishment: the tathagatagarbha mind (the mind in the state of tathagatagarbha) is limpid and ever quiescent, perfectly accomplished; hence the self-nature of perfect accomplishment.
The Tang translation says:
"Ignorance, craving, and karma — the various minds arise depending on them; thereby I understand this as the nature of dependent arising
(the self-nature of dependent arising)
. Falsely discriminating things as existent is what the deluded mind pursues; these distinctions are entirely nonexistent, yet delusion falsely counts them as existent
(the self-nature of false imagining)

. When the mind is bound by conditions, it arises in sentient beings; if conditions are far removed, I say nothing is seen. Having departed from all conditions, the marks discriminated by itself no longer arise in the body; this I call
(means)
no going. What arises in the minds of sentient beings — the grasping and the grasped — all that is seen is without mark; foolish people falsely discriminate, revealing the alaya
(the consciousness-store)
. The supreme storehouse consciousness, free from grasped and grasper, I call true suchness
(the self-nature of perfect accomplishment — the tathagatagarbha)

(Translation: Craving (clinging) born of ignorance, and karma — the various minds arise depending on them; thereby I understand that this is the self-nature of dependent arising. Falsely discriminating dharmas as existent is what the deluded mind pursues; in reality these myriad phenomena are without distinction (the true nature of all dharmas), yet the deluded mind falsely counts them as existent — this is the self-nature of false imagining. When the mind is bound by conditions, it arises in sentient beings; if conditions are far removed, I say nothing is seen. Having departed from all conditions, the marks discriminated by itself no longer arise in the body; this I call no going. What arises in the minds of sentient beings — the grasped and the grasping — all that is seen is in reality without mark, yet foolish people falsely discriminate various marks, and so the one mind becomes the evolving consciousnesses (the consciousness-store). The supreme storehouse consciousness, free from grasping and grasped, I call the self-nature of perfect accomplishment — the tathagatagarbha.)

(Revealing the alaya) Among the eight consciousnesses (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mental, manas, and alaya), the alaya is principal, and the other seven are all derived from it; therefore sutras and treatises often use it to represent the totality of the eight consciousnesses — the consciousness-store.
(The self-nature of perfect accomplishment) The tathagatagarbha. This sutra says:
"Mahamati, the bodhisattva mahasattva should be well versed in the three self-natures. What are the three self-natures? They are the imagined self-nature
(the self-nature of false imagining)
, the self-nature of dependent arising, and the accomplished self-nature
(the self-nature of perfect accomplishment)

. Mahamati, the self-nature of false imagining arises from marks. Mahamati said to the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, how does the self-nature of false imagining arise from marks?' The Buddha told Mahamati: 'The marks of the things of dependent arising, and the marks of things as they appear in activity — attachment to these gives rise to two kinds of self-nature of false imagining. These are established by the Tathagata, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One: namely, attachment to the marks of names, and attachment to the marks of things. Attachment to the marks of names means attachment to inner and outer dharmas. Attachment to the marks of things means attachment to the general and particular marks of just those inner and outer dharmas. These are called the two kinds of marks of the self-nature of false imagining. Whatever arises depending on a support or a condition is called dependent arising. What is the self-nature of accomplishment? It is freedom from the false imagining of the marks of names and the marks of things, what is attained by noble wisdom, and the realm reached by the conduct of self-realized noble wisdom; this is called the self-nature of accomplishment,
the tathagatagarbha mind
The Tang translation says:

"Mahamati, the bodhisattva mahasattva should well know the marks of the three self-natures. What are the three? They are: the self-nature of false imagining, the self-nature of dependent arising, and the self-nature of perfect accomplishment. Mahamati, the self-nature of false imagining arises from marks. How does it arise from marks? It is because one gives rise to attachment depending on the appearance of the various kinds of things of dependent arising. Mahamati, that attachment to the marks of things gives rise to two kinds of false imagining, which are proclaimed by all Tathagatas, namely: attachment to the marks of names, and attachment to the marks of things. Mahamati, attachment to the marks of things means attachment to inner and outer dharmas; attachment to the marks of names means attachment to the general and particular marks within those inner and outer dharmas. These are called the two kinds of marks of the self-nature of false imagining. Mahamati, what arises from a support and a condition is the nature of dependent arising. What is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment? It is the true suchness reached by self-realized noble wisdom, free from all discrimination of the marks of names and the marks of things. Mahamati,
this is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment, the tathagatagarbha mind

The relations among the three self-natures are: when the one mind is deluded about the self-nature of dependent arising of all dharmas and falsely grasps all dharmas as truly existent, it turns the tathagatagarbha into the eight consciousnesses (the consciousness-store); this is the self-nature of false imagining (the consciousness-store), and so one falls from Buddhahood into being a sentient being. When the one mind awakens to this self-nature of dependent arising and realizes the dharma of non-arising, it restores the eight consciousnesses (the consciousness-store) to the tathagatagarbha; this is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment (the tathagatagarbha), and so one goes from being a sentient being to Buddhahood.

Consciousness (the one mind) has two states, delusion and awakening. The state of delusion is the sentient being (among the ten dharma realms, all except the Buddha are called sentient beings); the state of awakening is the Buddha. Awakening is the original state of consciousness, called the storehouse consciousness, also named the tathagatagarbha; delusion is the state of ignorance in which consciousness flows through birth and death, called the evolving consciousnesses, also named the consciousness-store. Practice means returning to the source, restoring the evolving consciousnesses (the consciousness-store) to the storehouse consciousness (the tathagatagarbha).

(The ten dharma realms) Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, gods, hearers, solitary realizers, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The first six are the six ordinary realms; the last four are the four noble realms.
(The eight consciousnesses)
Eye consciousness, ear consciousness, nose consciousness, tongue consciousness, body consciousness, mental consciousness, manas consciousness, and alaya consciousness. (See
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathagatagarbha
in full.)
(The two selves)

"The self of persons" and "the self of dharmas," also called the two graspings, self-grasping and dharma-grasping. The self of persons (self-grasping): a person is a false combination of the five aggregates, arising when conditions gather and ceasing when conditions disperse; there is no real self-entity, yet sentient beings falsely grasp it as a truly existing self-entity. Breaking the self of persons, one ends segmental birth-and-death and escapes the round of rebirth. The self of dharmas (dharma-grasping): whether Buddhadharma or worldly dharma, all are falsely established depending on conditions and exist in mutual opposition; none has independent existence, yet sentient beings falsely grasp all dharmas as having truly existing essence and function. Breaking the self of dharmas, one ends transformational birth-and-death and perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. The Diamond Sutra says:
"If a bodhisattva comprehends the dharma of no-self, the Tathagata names him a true bodhisattva."

(The five aggregates) Also called the "five shadows." The five aggregates are: form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness — the five great elements that constitute body and mind. Among them, form refers to matter and is called "form-dharma"; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness belong to the mental and are called "mind-dharma." Form is the body; the remaining four are the mind. Master Yinguang said:

"The five shadows are form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Form is the body that is the karmic reward one has evoked; feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are the illusory, false mind that arises on contact with objects. Through these illusory body-and-mind dharmas, one gives rise to delusion and creates karma with respect to the objects of the six dusts."
(From the Essence of Master Yinguang's Writings) The Nirvana Sutra says:

"At the time of death, relatives weep. The person is terrified and cannot compose himself. All the good and evil of his life appear before him. After the warmth has gone, the past five aggregates cease and the present intermediate existence arises. After entering the womb, the present intermediate existence ceases and the future five aggregates arise. It is like a lamp arising and darkness ceasing, a lamp ceasing and darkness arising, continuous without interruption."
The Heart Sutra says:
"Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, when practicing deeply the prajna paramita, illuminated the five aggregates as all empty and crossed beyond all suffering and distress."

(Segmental birth-and-death) Sentient beings within the three realms and six paths, because of the good and evil karma they have evoked, all have a limited lifespan and a differentiated body; hence the name "segmental birth-and-death." One who ends segmental birth-and-death escapes the round of rebirth and leaves the three realms. (Transformational birth-and-death) The sages among the three vehicles have already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and have ended segmental birth-and-death. In the course of cultivating the path, deluded thoughts gradually cease and realization gradually increases; each period of this shift between delusion and awakening differs; the passage from the earlier into the later is just like one round of birth-and-death, so it is called "transformational birth-and-death." One who ends transformational birth-and-death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
(The two dharmas of existence and non-existence)

Existing dharmas and non-existing dharmas. Existing dharmas refer to the myriad phenomena of the world, all things. Non-existing dharmas refer to things that do not exist, such as turtle hair and rabbit horns. The "existence" here means that the mark exists; the "non-existence" means that the mark does not exist. Existence and non-existence are both spoken in relation to each other: non-existence is spoken in relation to existence, and existence in relation to non-existence. Since all dharmas are nothing whatsoever and originally not a single thing exists, to speak of existence or non-existence is entirely false view. (See
The True Nature of All Dharmas
in full.) The Wei translation says:

"Those of false views debate the arising of dharmas and falsely imagine existence and non-existence. If one knows there is nothing born, one also knows there is nothing ceasing. Seeing the world as all empty and quiescent, such a one does not fall into existence or non-existence."
Master Hanshan's Notes on Contemplating the Lankavatara Sutra says:

"Therefore this verse praises the Buddha as 'free from both existence and non-existence.' How profound! The two views of existence and non-existence are thorns in the dharmakaya. What is called self-realized noble wisdom is nothing else: one merely knows this and is free from this, and no real dharma is to be attained at all. This is indeed the ultimate doctrine of this sutra. A practitioner who knows this may be said to practice without practicing and realize without realizing. If for a single thought practice and realization are not forgotten, one falls back into this again — how much more so if one takes discriminating words and letters as attainment! If the observer observes in this way, he may be said to know the true nature of dharmas.'"

(Turtle hair and rabbit horns) This is only an analogy to illustrate the principle and should not be clung to one-sidedly; moreover, in the regions where the Buddha taught there were no green-haired turtles. And the so-called "green-haired turtle" is in fact a turtle on whose back algae grow, appearing as green filaments, which in the water merely look like turtle hair. ("Non-existence" means that the mark does not exist) The "mark" spoken of here means the manifestation of things in the dream of ignorance, which differs from the "mark" of daily life and natural science. Take air: daily life and natural science hold that it is colorless and without mark, but in Buddhadharma it has a mark, because its existence (within the dream of ignorance) can be determined by various means — only the naked eye cannot see it. In fact it has density, weight, cold and heat, motion and stillness; all of these are marks.
(Self-realized noble wisdom)
The Tathagata's wisdom of the essential nature of the dharma realm — the wisdom that awakens to "all dharmas are originally unborn"; also called the pure dharma-realm wisdom. This sutra says:

"Mahamati, one whose mark of the ultimate self-realized noble wisdom is such that he does not calculate or attach to any mark of dharma, gains the body of the samadhi of illusion, and advances and brings forth conduct at the stage of all Buddhas."
It also says:

"The Buddha told Mahamati: What former sages knew, they transmitted to one another — that false imagining has no nature. The bodhisattva mahasattva, dwelling alone in a quiet place, observes with self-realization, not relying on another, free from the views of false imagining, advances higher and higher, and enters the Tathagata's stage; this is called the mark of self-realized noble wisdom."
(The Tathagata's stage)
The stage of Buddhahood.
The sutra passage is taken from the Mahayana Sutra of Entering Lanka)

[Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling in the city of Lanka on the peak of Mount Malaya by the seashore, together with a great assembly of bhikshus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas.]

This is what I (Ananda) personally saw and heard. At that time, the Buddha was dwelling in the city of Lanka on the peak of Mount Malaya by the seashore, together with a great assembly of bhikshus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas.

(Thus have I heard) This is what I (Ananda) personally saw and heard. "Thus have I heard" engenders faith, proving that this sutra was indeed spoken by the Buddha and that the record is correct and without error. When the Buddha was about to enter nirvana, he instructed Venerable Ananda: when compiling the sutras, place the phrase "Thus have I heard" at the head of every sutra, to prove it was truly spoken by the Buddha and to distinguish it from the scriptures of other paths. The "I" is Ananda, the compiler of the sutras, referring to himself. Ananda was the Buddha's cousin, born on the night of the Buddha's enlightenment. Later he left home to follow the Buddha and became his attendant, famed for never forgetting what he heard and for being foremost in learning. When Ananda left home, the Buddha had already taught the Dharma for twenty years, so he asked the Buddha to repeat all that had been taught before; he also attained the samadhi of self-realization of the dharma-nature, by which he could comprehend all dharmas in samadhi. Therefore after the Buddha's parinirvana, when Venerable Mahakashyapa assembled the sutra collection in the great stone cave of Magadha, five hundred arhats gathered, and the assembly urged Ananda to ascend the seat and repeat the sutras. In the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha says:

"I and Ananda and others, at the place of King of Emptiness Buddha, simultaneously brought forth the aspiration for anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Ananda always delighted in much learning, while I always strove diligently. Therefore I have already attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, while Ananda protects and upholds my Dharma, and will also protect the Dharma-treasury of future Buddhas, teaching and bringing to accomplishment the assembly of bodhisattvas."

(At one time) At that time — the time when the Buddha taught this sutra, when teacher and disciples were in accord in the Way and the capacities of beings and the teaching met. The Tathagata's teaching of the Dharma reaches humans and gods, and its compilation and transmission spread throughout the world; because years, months, and days cannot be made to agree, "at one time" records it. (Teacher and disciples) Teacher and student, master and disciple. (The capacities of beings and the teaching meeting) "Capacity" is the root-capacity of the listeners; "teaching" is the Buddha's bestowal of teaching. Root-capacities differ, so the Buddha, according to their capacities, bestows teachings of greater or lesser depth. "The capacities of beings and the teaching meeting" means that the roots of the listeners at the assembly and the Buddha's teaching respond and accord. (Buddha) Short for "Buddha," here meaning Shakyamuni Buddha. "Buddha" is a Sanskrit sound, rendered in Chinese as "the Awakened One." Inwardly awakened, one is without any false thoughts; outwardly awakened, one is unstained by the six dusts.

(Great bhikshu) "Bhikshu" is the general term for one who has left home and received the complete precepts; males are called "bhikshus," females "bhikshunis." A "great bhikshu" is a bhikshu of lofty virtue and senior years. (Great bodhisattva) Those from the first ground upward are great bodhisattvas. A "great bhikshu" is a bhikshu of lofty virtue and senior years. (Great bodhisattva) Those from the first ground upward are great bodhisattvas.

[These bodhisattva mahasattvas had all already comprehended the five dharmas, the three natures, the various consciousnesses, and no-self, and were well aware of the meaning that realms are the mind's own manifestation. They sported in the boundless powers of the samadhis and spiritual penetrations of perfect ease, and according to the minds of sentient beings manifested various forms, skillfully taming them. All Buddhas poured water on their crowns with their own hands. They all came to this assembly from various Buddha-lands, and the bodhisattva mahasattva Mahamati was foremost among them.]

These great bodhisattvas had all comprehended the five dharmas, the three self-natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two no-selves, and understood the principle that realms are the mind's own manifestation. With the boundless powers of the samadhis and spiritual penetrations of perfect ease, they sported in the three realms, and according to the minds of sentient beings manifested corresponding forms to skillfully tame and deliver them. All Buddhas with their own hands poured water on their crowns. They all came to this assembly from various Buddha-lands, and the bodhisattva mahasattva Mahamati was foremost among them.

(Sporting) When Buddhas and bodhisattvas sport in spiritual penetrations, transforming people as their own delight, this is called "sporting." (Skillful means) The devices, methods, or words adopted to guide and teach sentient beings. (Manifesting various forms) Displaying various bodily forms. As the Universal Gateway Chapter says:
"This Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva has accomplished such merit and virtue, and with various forms travels through all lands, delivering sentient beings."
(Foremost) The leading position in the assembly is called foremost. Sometimes one person is foremost, sometimes several.
